reading.title: The printer
reading.text:
The printer in our office is old. It stops every week, and every week somebody says we should buy a new one.

On Monday the printer stopped again. Marta looked at it for a minute. Then she opened it, took out one small piece of paper, and closed it. The printer worked.

Nobody talks about buying a new printer now. They just ask Marta.

questions.q: How often does the printer stop?

reading.title: Two weeks, probably
reading.text:
Every developer has been asked how long something will take, and every developer has given a number that turned out to be wrong. This is not because they are careless. It is because the question is being asked before the work has been looked at properly, and an estimate made then is really a guess with a job title.

The useful answer is not a smaller number. It is a different sentence: "Two weeks if the database is what I think it is, and I will know that by Wednesday." That gives the person asking something they can plan around, and it gives the person answering permission to be wrong about the part they genuinely cannot see yet.

The teams that do this well are not better at guessing. They are better at saying which part of the guess is soft.

options: They are made before the work is understood

questions.q: What does the writer say a useful answer includes?
What are good teams better at?

reading.title: Paying it down
reading.text:
Technical debt is one of the few metaphors in software that has survived contact with reality, and it has survived because the analogy holds all the way down. You take a shortcut today and receive something valuable immediately: the feature ships, the customer is happy, the quarter closes well. What you have actually done is borrow, and the repayments begin quietly the following week.

The interest is paid in a currency nobody puts on a dashboard. Every subsequent change takes slightly longer. Every new person takes slightly longer to understand the system. Nobody can point at the moment it became expensive, because it never did; it became expensive gradually, in increments too small to argue about individually.

What separates teams that manage this from teams that drown in it is not discipline, and it is certainly not a rule against shortcuts — shortcuts are frequently correct. It is whether the debt was taken deliberately and written down. A shortcut somebody chose, recorded, and scheduled to repay is a financing decision. The same shortcut taken silently, because it was Friday and everyone wanted to go home, is just a mess with a deadline attached.

questions.q: Why does the writer say the metaphor holds?
options: The repayments are real and ongoing

questions.q: What distinguishes teams that manage debt well?
options: They take it deliberately and record it
